newsitem.title: USA: SEC's Hunt questions muni bond lawyers' leadership.
newsitem.headline: SEC's Hunt questions muni bond lawyers' leadership.

text.p: Municipal bond lawyers should take a more "aggressive leadership role" in curbing improper political contributions and telling clients up front whether they will help protect them from securities law violations, an SEC member said late Wednesday.

In a speech before the Bond Club of Virginia, SEC member Isaac Hunt conceded that the National Association of Bond Lawyers (NABL) has told members publicly not to give political contributions in return for muni bond business.
But NABL has never even said that there is a "pay-to-play" problem with lawyers, Hunt said. And its only solution is for lawyers to continue to rely on state campaign diclosure laws, Hunt said.

Moreover, Hunt said, lawyers that responded to a 1996 NABL survey on pay-to-play, opposed following in the steps of Wall Street firms that signed a voluntary ban in 1995 on dealer contributions to state and local officials.
"NABL's reaction to the survey results was to follow and not lead; the NABL board decided to not press the pay-to-play issue," Hunt said.
He lauded the Association of the Bar of the City of New York for proposing a professional disciplinary rule to restrict broadly pay-to-play practices in New York State.
Hunt also said bond lawyers must be clear in their retainers with new muni clients about whether they will review official statements for potential securities law violations.
He said bond counsel cannot "woo potential clients with an expansive list of services" they pledge to perform, then retreat if the deal comes under scrutiny by regulators.

"If an attorney promises a client that he or she will perform certain services, such as reviewing an OS for potential securities law issues, then that lawyer should follow through, perform those services, and take responsibility for the quality of those services," Hunt said.

Hunt cited stinging remarks by U.S. District Judge William Young during a sentencing hearing last month for municipal bond dealer Mark Ferber, who was convicted on graft and kickback charges involving bond dealers.
"I am simply appalled at the level of practice of the municipal bond lawyers that I have heard about in this case," Hunt said, quoting Young.

"There is no stronger advocate of a free, vigorous, independent, professional bar in the U.S. than this member of it," the Young quote continued. "But I sat here and heard the most sorry, evasive explications and excuses for legal advice," the quote adds.
Hunt said bond issuers today expect objective bond opinions from their counsel, "not partisan advocacy pieces based upon plausible arguments."
"Many issuers - especially small issuers - look to bond counsel's advice as the voice of objective experience, and follow such advice to the letter."
He said he is "troubled" about press reports that bond lawyers are counseling clients to make only the bare minimum of disclosures required by SEC rules for their bond offering documents and updates.
